newsitem.title: UK: Major, grey man on the high wire of power.
newsitem.headline: Major, grey man on the high wire of power.

text.p: John Major, the son of a trapeze artist, has performed one of the toughest juggling acts in politics by surviving for 6-1/2 years as prime minister while his Conservative party tore itself apart over Europe.
The working class boy who took over a party traditionally run by the upper classes from the Iron Lady, Margaret Thatcher, has been accused of weak leadership, a lack of vision and a charisma deficit.

But the grey-haired, grey-suited Major has shown inner steel by winning the three greatest challenges of his high-wire political career. The May 1 election he announced on Monday is his biggest test yet.

If he were to lead the Conservatives -- 25 points behind Tony Blair's moderate Labour Party in opinion polls -- to an unprecedented fifth successive victory, it would be one of the most staggering achievements in British political history.

When the Conservatives dumped the increasingly autocratic Margaret Thatcher in November 1990 after 11 years in office, the inexperienced Major emerged as a compromise candidate and the party's best hope of winning the next election.

He was Thatcher's chosen heir, even if she did later undermine his attempts to keep his party together by sniping from the sidelines. Taking to his much-mocked soap box to appeal directly to voters, he defied the odds and the polls by winning the April 1992 election. Voters preferred "honest John" to leaping into the unknown by picking Neil Kinnock's Labour Party.
He pledged to create a classless society in a "nation at ease with itself" and to put Britain "at the heart of Europe".

But ties with the European Union have proved his undoing. Sterling's ignominious withdrawal from the European currency grid in September 1992 triggered open warfare in Conservative ranks about how closely Britain should tie itself to the EU.

Ironically it was Major, as finance minister, who persuaded Thatcher, against her better judgement, to join the grid. Major was forced to shift to the right to pacify so-called Eurosceptics in his party who feared the influence exerted by Brussels and openly defied him in parliament.

Finally, in June 1995 the patience of a man renowned for his sang-froid snapped. In a dramatic news conference he told his right-wing opponents to "put up or shut up" and resigned the Conservative party leadership.

His gamble worked, to a degree. He beat former cabinet minister John Redwood but the Eurosceptics were not silenced and members of parliament continued to bicker in public, dismaying millions of grass-root Conservative voters.

Major was mercilessly mocked for a "Back to Basics" morality campaign, one of the few policies over the five-year government that carried his imprimatur. It backfired amid a flurry of sex scandals and sleaze allegations about Conservative MPs.

But he fought doggedly to bring peace to Northern Ireland, one of the 20th century's most insoluble guerrilla conflicts, even though the campaign provided few political gains and now appears to be melting into the sectarian sand.
His diffidence proved an effective weapon as much as a hindrance. He reacted with calm when Irish Republican Army guerrillas mortar bombed his Downing Street residence in 1991.
"Gentlemen, I think we had better move to another room," he told cabinet colleagues.
His quiet authority during the Gulf War, shortly after he took power, sent his popularity soaring. "Don't forget I am an Englishman. The English tend to be understated," he once said.
One commentator said Major "melted into the foreground". His sacked finance minister Norman Lamont once witheringly accused his close friend of being "in office but not in power."

Major, born in south London on March 29, 1943, saw poverty firsthand as a child. His father, originally a trapeze artist in a vaudeveille act, had a factory making garden gnome ornaments that went bankrupt, forcing the Majors to swap their family home for a modest apartment.
Like Thatcher, whose father was a small-town shopkeeper, Major's upbringing contrasted sharply with those of past Conservative leaders, wealthy and with estates in the country.
He left school at 16 and did several jobs before going into banking. He worked in Hong Kong and Nigeria where he suffered a serious leg injury in a car crash that still affects his walk.

Major entered parliament in 1979 as member for Huntingdon, north of London. He was spotted by Conservative talent scouts working in local politics in the working class London suburb of Lambeth, a Labour Party stronghold.
He rose to become Minister of Social Security and in 1987 Chief Secretary (junior minister) to the Treasury.
Major was then unexpectedly catapulted into the spotlight when Thatcher made him Foreign Secretary in July 1989.

Three months later, he became Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance Minister), articulating Thatcher's anti-inflation policy and his own gradualist approach to European Monetary Union. He is Britain's youngest premier of the 20th century.
Major's private passion is sport. He regularly attends Chelsea soccer club games and has the results of cricket internationals relayed to his plane when he is away on foreign trips.

Major's wife Norma, whom he married in 1970, is an opera fan. In 1987, she published a biography of Australian soprano Joan Sutherland and did much to promote a boost in opera's popularity. The Majors have two children, Elizabeth and James.
